ety.text: From Middle English nave, navye, from Anglo-Norman, Old French navie, from Latin nāvigia < nāvigium, from Latin nāvigō, nāvis (“boat”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare Ancient Greek ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), Persian ناو (nâv, “boat, warship”), Sanskrit नाव (nāva, “ship”), Old English nōwend (“mariner, sailor”). By surface analysis, Latin nav- + -y. Displaced native Old English sċiphere (literally “ship army”).

senses.d: A country's entire maritime military force, including ships and personnel.
ex: People who get seasick easily shouldn't join the navy.

senses.d: A governmental department in charge of a country's maritime military force.
Any fleet of maritime vessels, and especially the entire fleet of any particular nationality, including vessels that are commercial, military, or both.
A dark blue colour, usually called navy blue.
Having the dark blue colour of navy blue.
ex: The cover is as navy as a bruise.
The morning shadow on his chin was almost as navy as his heavy-lidded eyes, his cheekbones exquisitely sculptured in his haughty face.

senses.d: Belonging to the navy; typical of the navy.
ex: It was not what you would picture as a typical meeting with a naval officer. In fact, it was about as navy as an Abbott and Costello movie.
Goodwin was navy through and through.

grp.label: having a navy (dark blue) colour — see also light blue, blue
